news.originalContent:
The country’s largest Muslim advocacy group urges Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims instead of attacking its efforts.

The largest Muslim civil liberties organisation in the United States has condemned suggestions by President Donald Trump that it could face a blanket designation as a “terrorist” group.

The Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR) said the White House should be addressing violence against American Muslims, rather than attacking the rights group.

“The Trump administration should focus on addressing this surge in violent hate, not entertaining smears against the civil rights organisation that counters such hate,” CAIR said in a statement to Al Jazeera on Tuesday.

On Monday, Trump said he was considering giving a blanket “terrorist” designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and that his administration was also looking at CAIR, which is already classified as a “terrorist” group in Texas and Florida.

“CAIR is another one we are watching,” he said of the organisation.

When asked if he was considering naming CAIR as a foreign “terrorist” group, he responded: “I’m not going to say that yet, but it could happen.”

In its statement, CAIR said that it was “fully prepared to defend our civil rights work and the broader American Muslim community from any new attempts to censor free speech, punish dissent or otherwise undermine the rule of law”.

“Our advocacy for justice here and abroad is the real reason that anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian extremists spend so much time obsessing over our work,” it said.

Trump’s comments on Monday came during an exchange with reporters outside the White House, following a question about Egypt’s crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood and whether Washington would consider a broader designation of the group.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration designated the Muslim Brotherhood chapters in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as foreign “terrorist” organisations.

Trump praised Egypt, where the Muslim Brotherhood originated, for cracking down on the group, indicating it did so at his request.

“Egypt has clamped down very hard on the Muslim Brotherhood, at my request,” he told reporters as he left the White House on Monday.

“Egypt did a great job,” Trump said.

news.originalContent:
The law targets the group’s financing and activities as renewed fighting threatens to derail efforts to end Yemen’s war.

Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a law designating the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising the group’s activities and financing, as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government.

The vote, held over two sessions by videolink on Monday, comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. Parliament said it had deferred the bill, first tabled at a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, to give peace efforts a chance.

It noted that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the Iranian-backed group of brushing aside “all options for peace”.

Yemen’s cabinet approved the draft law on October 11. The country’s National Defence Council had designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States also lists the group as a “terrorist” organisation, and Saudi Arabia treats it as one.

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the legislation was formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, on Tuesday to be signed into law.

It runs to 55 articles and designates the group – including all of its political, military and civilian formations – “a terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction”.

It also toughens penalties for offences including seizing state authority, besieging cities, attacking civilians, laying landmines and attacking international shipping. Certain offences would carry the death penalty.

The law also sets out procedures to identify, trace, freeze and confiscate assets linked to the group and its affiliated entities.

The vote comes amid months of renewed hostilities after several years of relative calm on Yemen’s front lines. In late June, the Houthis announced an escalation against government forces and Saudi Arabia, saying the move was aimed at lifting what the group describes as a “blockade”.

In early September, a Houthi ground offensive on the western coast gave the group control of parts of Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after government forces withdrew from the port city of Mocha and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area.

Government forces launched an operation called “Dawn of Yemen” in early October to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. news.originalContent:
France witnesses its third major public sector strike since September, as protests highlight wage and service concerns.

Demonstrators have gathered across France after unions called a nationwide strike by public sector workers in a bid to secure pay rises, as protests over living standards and squeezed public services continue to roil the country.

France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were urged to mobilise on Tuesday after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands for across-the-board pay rises, following last week’s minimum wage boost for private-sector workers.

It is the third united day of strikes and protests in the public sector since September, after a previous mobilisation earlier this month drew hundreds of thousands of workers and saw police fire tear gas as clashes broke out in several cities.

More unions joined the call to strike after Lecornu’s meeting, saying the government’s proposed measures did not address what they describe as an urgent pay and cost-of-living crisis. In Paris, a major rally was taking place in the east of the city, with dozens of other demonstrations planned nationwide.

Police sources told AFP that between 40,000 and 80,000 people were expected to demonstrate in the capital, and up to 300,000 across France. In Paris, university professor Nicolas Prevot said he was marching to defend human rights, protect public services and keep the far right from power in next year’s presidential election.

news.originalContent:
Online petition with more than 32,000 signatures demands the university ‘cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak’.

Thousands of people have signed a petition and protests are planned at the University of Oxford against the appearance of Nathan Cofnas, an American academic and self-described “race realist” accused of racism.

Cofnas, who had accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism last July, is due to give a talk at Oxford’s Oriel College on Tuesday evening at an event organised by the Oxford Reform student society, which is linked to the far-right Reform UK party.

Cofnas has drawn controversy for years with his eugenics-linked views tying race to intelligence, writing that Black people were less intelligent than others in an article which led to his dismissal from his position at a college at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

He was suspended as a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University in Belgium in August after making plagiarism allegations against Arday, a Black Cambridge professor. Arday consistently denied allegations of plagiarism but acknowledged errors in his work.

Arday was later found dead in his home after resigning his post amid the ballooning scandal.

Cofnas was later allowed to resume some academic work at Ghent remotely, without teaching, while an investigation continued.

The Oxford Reform student society defended its event – titled “Is DEI Undermining Higher Education?”, referring to diversity, equity and inclusion – and said it is “committed to broadening participation in university life”.

In a statement, Oxford University said the event being hosted on its grounds “does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers”.

An online petition demanding the university “cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak” has more than 32,000 signatures.

“Ideas platformed at Oxford do not stay in the lecture theatre”, the petition said.

news.originalContent:
Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.

Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade.

The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104.

Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday.

The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies.

But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations.

Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.”

He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.”

Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities.

“All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter.

Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity.

“We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session.

He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested.

The swearing-in session also marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government.

Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections.

The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles.

Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years.

Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work.

“Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.”

In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session.

“Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

news.originalContent:
A major health organisation declares measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, reversing a public health achievement maintained for 26 years, as the country grapples with its largest outbreak in more than three decades.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), declared measles endemic in the US, Bolivia, and Mexico on Tuesday after determining that the same strain of the virus had circulated continuously in the country for at least 12 months.

An international panel of experts that advises PAHO on the prevalence of measles and rubella “recommended that the measles elimination status be withdrawn,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, “a recommendation which I have accepted.”

Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000.

PAHO’s announcement follows a review of epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The US has recorded approximately 7,700 measles infections since the beginning of 2025, according to CDC figures.

It is the highest number of cases the country has seen in more than 30 years. The climbing numbers come as vaccine hesitancy has grown under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has repeatedly cast doubt on the safety of vaccines despite scientific evidence to the contrary.

“This is hard to see happen,” he said. “But at the same time it is predictable when you don’t have experts running a public healthcare system.”

news.originalContent:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel will appear before three joint House panels for closed-door testimonies in early December, three committees announced Tuesday.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party for transcribed interviews on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2. The former CEO resigned on Thursday following allegations that he had an affair with a Chinese spy.

House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chairman John Moolenaar said in a joint statement that they are seeking answers about Huang’s potential national security breach.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” the chairmen said. “The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.” (RELATED: Jensen Huang Agrees To Testify Before Congress Over Relationship With Alleged Chinese Spy)

🚨🚨 Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will testify before the House Permanent Select Committee of Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1 and 2. Both testimonies will be transcribed. @DailyCaller

Huang agreed to testify Thursday about the alleged relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese asset and former executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips. Nvidia formed a committee Tuesday to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, CBS News reported.

Lawmakers and Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent expressed concern that China is gaining access to the company’s advanced chips, which are critical to developing artificial intelligence (AI) models. The U.S. barred sales of Nvidia’s chips to China over national security concerns.

“Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement.

President Donald Trump was reportedly informed of Alice Huang’s ties to China in 2025 but took no action. The Department of Justice (DOJ) overtook the criminal investigation into Megaspeed following an email from Teter to the Commerce Department, The New York Times reported Monday.

news.originalContent:
US President Trump said the deals would prevent ‘coercion by any single foreign supplier’.

United States President Donald Trump says that members of the Quad, a security grouping of the US and three Indo-Pacific countries, have reached agreements aimed at securing supply chains of critical minerals.

Trump met India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi – the other Quad leaders – in the Philippines on Thursday.

“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in remarks ahead of the meeting in Manila.

During the meeting, Trump said the agreements on critical minerals aimed to prevent “coercion by any single foreign supplier”. He did not single out China, which dominates global rare earth supplies.

Trump later said the US would have “everything we need” on rare earths in 10 months.

“We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before. We’re going to catch them [China] within 10 months,” he said.

China last year imposed restrictions on exports of rare earths amid a trade dispute with the US. In June, the two sides agreed a deal aimed at restoring the US’s access to China’s rare earth supplies.

In a statement after the leaders’ meeting, the Quad expressed “grave concerns” about “economic coercion”, including through arbitrary export restrictions.

While the statement did not name any country, the US and Japan have complained about China’s restrictions on ‌exports of rare earths vital to the manufacturing of everything from electric cars to mobile phones.

China has effectively shut off exports of key critical minerals to Japan for nearly a year as relations between Asia’s two largest economies have nosedived.

It was Trump’s first meeting of the Quad grouping – which his predecessor US President Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the meeting suggested the Quad grouping had a “functioning relationship”.

“Given the damage to the Quad during the Trump administration, including the instability caused by Trump’s tariffs on India, and India’s response by diversifying, the Quad meeting and statements like this give reassurance that there is still a functioning relationship,” Lucas said. “I’m not sure I’d call it an alliance, as I don’t think the Trump folks believe in alliances.”

Trump also joined a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila on the first day of a three-day trip to Asia.

After the Philippines, Trump will travel to China and attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where he is expected to hold a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.

Asked by reporters about a CNN report which claimed that US intelligence had determined Tehran was developing plans to use a so-called “dirty bomb” to target officials in the Trump administration, Trump said he was “looking into it”.

He said that if Iran posed an “imminent threat” to Washington, “they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before”.

He added that he “hoped” Iran did not pose a threat, but that he took such a scenario “very seriously” because “they happen to be crazy”.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghei said in a post on X that “Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations, including the recent claims published by The New York Times and the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged ‘dirty bomb’ propagated by CNN.”

news.originalContent:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is cracking down on dangerous military barracks conditions that have plagued American troops for decades, as he faces mounting political backlash and sinking approval ratings.

Hegseth has ordered military leaders to address emergency housing conditions within 24 hours or relocate affected service members, while giving the military departments five days to demonstrate compliance, according to a recent memo. The long-overdue crackdown comes as the secretary faces growing scrutiny over the unpopular Iran war and a potential impeachment vote, with a recent Common Defense poll of military members and veterans finding majorities disapproved of his leadership.

Fifty-four percent of active-duty U.S. service members and 64% of military family members disapproved of Hegseth, according to the October survey conducted for Common Defense by Change Research.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment on why this matter is just being addressed now and what else the administration has done to resolve the issue. (RELATED: Iran War Sparks Explosive Town Hall Between Navy Brass, Military Families)

Why the rush on the Barracks? Immediate Action on Unacceptable Living Conditions in Unaccompanied Housing - Inspections of all barracks due by Monday https://t.co/ZESJk4x6ai

“Every Service member deserves a place to live that is clean, safe, and comfortable. The Military Departments must act with urgency to correct unacceptable living conditions, reinforce confidence that concerns will be addressed, and strengthen readiness,” Hegseth wrote in the Nov 10. memo.

By Nov 13., the memo was updated to require that all military branches report actions taken to improve living conditions to the newly formed Barracks Task Force. They are also required to provide a projected timeline to restore rooms to “habitable occupancy” and address any policy or resource barriers that require Pentagon resolution, per Military Times.

The Barracks Task Force is led by Medal of Honor recipient, and senior Hegseth advisor Dakota Meyer. Meyer has thus far visited seven bases to tour barracks and talk to service members living in them. He is slated to visit 30 by the end of December, Military Times reports.

Unlivable barracks conditions — including dirty tap water, methane gas leaks from cracked sewage pipes, and moldy bedrooms — have plagued the military for years.

This memo came at the same time the Iran war is rapidly losing support and one week after Hegseth faced a failed impeachment effort.

news.originalContent:
پنج کشور عضو اتحادیه اروپا قصد دارند سال آینده مرکزی برای اخراج مهاجران در روآندا راه‌اندازی کنند. این اقدام بخشی از تلاش گسترده‌تر آنها برای افزایش روند بازگرداندن مهاجران است. بر اساس بیانیه‌های دولت‌های هلند و دانمارک، انتظار می‌رود آلمان، دانمارک، اتریش، یونان و هلند در سال ۲۰۲۷ یک «مرکز بازگشت» راه‌اندازی کنند که آماده پذیرش افرادی باشد که از این کشورها به آنجا منتقل خواهند شد.

این کشورها اعلام کردند که این طرح شامل مهاجرانی خواهد شد که به‌طور غیرقانونی در کشورهای آن‌ها اقامت دارند و مشمول حکم اخراج شده‌اند. دولت هلند نیز می‌گوید که این مرکز می‌تواند جایگزینی برای مواردی باشد که امکان بازگرداندن افراد اخراج‌شده به کشور مبدأشان وجود ندارد.

به گفته این کشورهای اروپایی، افرادی که به روآندا منتقل می‌شوند، می‌توانند یا در جامعه میزبان ادغام شوند و اقامت خود را در آنجا ادامه دهند، یا به کشور خود بازگردند. این طرح شامل افرادی خواهد شد که تمام راه‌های قانونی برای دریافت اجازه اقامت در این پنج کشور را طی کرده و دیگر امکان قانونی برای ماندن ندارند.

این موضوع با توافق لغوشده بریتانیا با روآندا تفاوت دارد؛ توافقی که بر اساس آن قرار بود افراد به روآندا فرستاده شوند تا درخواست‌های پناهندگی آن‌ها در آنجا بررسی شود. چالش‌های حقوقی باعث شدند توافق بریتانیا هرگز به مرحله اجرا نرسد و سرانجام در سال ۲۰۲۴، دولت تازه‌روی‌کارآمده حزب کارگر آن را لغو کرد.

اما اکنون دفتر نخست‌وزیری بریتانیا احتمال پیوستن این کشور به طرح جدید را رد نکرده و اعلام کرده است که این برنامه را «با علاقه دنبال خواهد کرد».

این پنج کشور می‌گویند طرح انتقال مهاجران به خارج از اروپا با قوانین اتحادیه اروپا و حقوق بین‌الملل مطابقت دارد؛ اما نهادهای حقوق بشری معتقدند که چنین اقدامی ممکن است حقوق مهاجران را نقض کند.

روز دوشنبه ۱۶ نوامبر/۲۵ آبان، در یک کنفرانس خبری مشترک در وین، کریستیان اشتوکر، صدراعظم اتریش، گفت که هدف این پنج کشور، کاهش فشار بر نظام‌های پناهندگی اروپا و متوقف‌کردن فعالیت قاچاقچیانی است که سفرهای مرگبار از طریق دریای مدیترانه را سازمان‌دهی می‌کنند.

دولت هلند هم در بیانیه‌ای اعلام کرد که در مرحله نخست این توافق، تنها مردان مجرد به کشورهای خارج از اروپا فرستاده خواهند شد. هلند همچنین گفته تمرکز خود را بر افرادی خواهد گذاشت که از کشورهای مبدأ واقع در همان منطقه جغرافیایی روآندا می‌آیند.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

وینسنت بیروتا، وزیر کشور روآندا، گفته است که کشورش متعهد به همکاری با شرکای اروپایی برای ارائه راه‌حلی «امن، قانونی و شرافتمندانه برای مهاجران» است.

پیش از اعلام رسمی این توافق، منابع دیپلماتیک به خبرگزاری فرانسه گفتند که انتظار می‌رود این مرکز در ابتدا به‌صورت آزمایشی فعالیت کند و میزبان حدود ۱۰۰ نفر باشد. بر این اساس، احتمال دارد هر یک از پنج کشور حدود ۲۰ مهاجر را به روآندا بفرستد.

کلمانتین دو مونتژوا، پژوهشگر ارشد بخش آفریقا در سازمان دیده‌بان حقوق بشر، در واکنش به این خبر گفته انتخاب روآندا به‌عنوان محل این مرکز نگران‌کننده است؛ زیرا این کشور سابقه‌ای شناخته‌شده در سرکوب مخالفان، بازداشت‌های خودسرانه، بدرفتاری با زندانیان و حمایت از شورشیان مسلح در جمهوری دموکراتیک کنگو، کشور همسایه خود، دارد.

او گفت: «پرداخت پول به دولت کیگالی برای میزبانی از یک برنامه اخراج مهاجران، نه‌تنها موجب رنج و آسیب‌دیدن افرادی خواهد شد که به آنجا فرستاده می‌شوند، بلکه منابع مالی و اهرم فشار سیاسی در اختیار دولتی قرار می‌دهد که مسئول نقض جدی حقوق بشر، هم در داخل کشور خود و هم در خارج از آن است.»

با نزدیک‌شدن انتخابات در چندین کشور عضو اتحادیه اروپا، دولت‌ها تحت فشار قرار گرفته‌اند تا نشان دهند توانایی کنترل مهاجرت را دارند. بر اساس آمار آژانس اروپایی گارد مرزی و ساحلی، در ۱۰ ماه نخست سال ۲۰۲۶ نزدیک به ۱۱۰ هزار مورد عبور غیرقانونی از مرزهای اتحادیه اروپا ثبت شده است. این رقم در مقایسه با مدت مشابه سال قبل، ۲۹ درصد کاهش نشان می‌دهد.

در ماه اکتبر گذشته، حدود ۱۸ هزار و ۱۰۰ مورد عبور از مرزهای اروپا شناسایی شد که تقریباً ۶ درصد کمتر از اکتبر ۲۰۲۵، اما ۲۲ درصد بیشتر از ماه سپتامبر بود. به گفته این آژانس، افزایش اخیر عمدتاً به دلیل رشد چشمگیر ورود مهاجران از مسیر غرب آفریقا به سمت جزایر قناری بوده است.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Cindy Ord/Getty Images for Teen Vogue)

Prominent Right-wingers critical of President Donald Trump clashed over the weekend regarding what it means to be an anti-Trump conservative as the movement grapples with the Democrats’ blue wave in the midterms and the approaching end of the Trump era.

The exchange began Thursday after a video surfaced of Sarah Longwell, co-founder of Republican advocacy group Defending Democracy Together and founder and publisher of The Bulwark, describing herself as a “lib” while celebrating the Democrats’ election victory at the “What’s Next” conference hosted by the Majority Democrats group last Thursday, Nov. 12 in Denver, Colorado. (RELATED: Trump’s White House Counsel Draws Line Against Dems’ Potential Abuse Of Power After Congress Flips Blue)

“You may know us; we’re the Never Trumpers. At least we were ten years ago. Now we’re just kind of libs, just like the rest of you,” Longwell said, attempting to get the crowd animated.

The video prompted a response from Babylon Bee writer Frank Fleming, who asked who is crazier: “People who surrendered all their principles to always agree with Trump or people who surrendered all their principles to always oppose him?”

The Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell at Democrat conference: "You may know us, we’re the Never Trumpers. At least we were ten years ago. Now we’re just kind of libs just like the rest of you." Yes, we know. https://t.co/ikdUQdUyHU

Jonah Goldberg, editor-in-chief of the center-right, Never Trump digital media company, argued that both the Always Trump and Never Trump mentalities were two sides of the same coin.

Longwell took issue with the comparison, responding to Goldberg by framing “anti-anti Trumpers and far leftists as two sides of the same coin.”

She argued that both groups understood Trump’s opponent in the 2024 election, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris, “would be better for the country than Trump,” but Republicans critical of Trump “refused to say so and spent their energy shitting on normie dems.”

“And now that Trump is catastrophic, they’re all trying to wave away the role their moral ambivalence played in getting us here,” Longwell continued. “This is all just classic ‘People will forgive you for being wrong, but they’ll never forgive you for being right.’”

Goldberg fired back Sunday, calling Longwell a “political operative” who would “say or do what’s necessary for your team to win.”

I walked away from this stupid spat for a day. So I missed this. Sarah, if you honestly think this “anti-anti Trump” sophomoric bullshit is a thoughtful or clever response to me or description of how I’ve behaved the last decade, I honestly think you are so deep in your bubble that any and all of your political and moral judgement is simply worthless. I don’t even want to bother arguing with you, I’m more embarrassed for you than anything else. But I’ll engage one more time. Look, the reason for the Bulwark’s current orientation is evaporating as we’re reaching the end of the Trump era. It appears to me and everybody else that during your bow-taking moment the other day you tried to advance your rebranding when you told a room full of conventional progressive Dems that you were a “lib” just like them. People noticed. They pointed out that you conceded the central criticism of your project. But as you still need to hold onto some vestige of your “conserving conservatism” schtick you tried to clean up your remarks by suggesting you meant “classical liberal.” Literally no one believes that’s what you meant, including obviously the people in that room, and I doubt many believe you’re a classical liberal (is there a chapter of “Classical Liberals For Abdul Syed” I missed?). The way you frame this makes my point, not yours. You’re a political operative. You think, like a political operative, that you should say or do what’s necessary for your team to win. That’s entirely defensible for political operatives and party hacks (within reason, I have no patience for Trump apologists and hacks. I can show you the receipts if you don’t believe me). But here’s the point: I’m neither a political operative nor party hack. Kamala Harris would have been better than Trump, happy to say it. But you pretty clearly think that means I should have become a partisan for her and spin for her and Democrats the way you do. I don’t want to be a partisan hack. It’s not for me. But you cannot even comprehend such motives. All you have is a hammer and so everything is a nail to you. Projecting your self-serving bullshit on me doesn’t mean it’s not bullshit, no matter how good it makes you feel. I’m glad I could clear this up for you.

While Goldberg stressed that he had no patience for Trump apologists and hacks, he distinguished himself as “neither a political operative nor party hack.”

“Kamala Harris would have been better than Trump, happy to say it. But you pretty clearly think that means I should have become a partisan for her and spin for her and Democrats the way you do. I don’t want to be a partisan hack. It’s not for me. But you cannot even comprehend such motives,” Goldberg said. “All you have is a hammer, and so everything is a nail to you. Projecting your self-serving bullshit on me doesn’t mean it’s not bullshit, no matter how good it makes you feel.”

The back-and-forth involved plenty of personal attacks, but the dispute goes beyond a personality clash. It exposes an existential crisis of purpose and business models within the fracturing Never Trump movement, as the political glue that has held it together approaches its expiration date.

As the Trump era moves closer to its end, each faction of the movement must look toward 2028 and decide whether to maintain its existing alliances or adapt to whatever emerges as the new political landscape.

news.originalContent:
A forensic scientist spent over a year studying and analyzing Jeffrey Epstein’s autopsy photographs and does not believe the infamous pedophile’s 2019 death was a suicide.

Dr. Michael Freeman is a consultant in forensic medicine who studies homicides, and was given rare access to the autopsy photos by the dead child sex trafficker’s brother Mark Epstein, the New York Times reported Monday. After looking at the first photograph, Freeman immediately thought something was off.

“The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” Freeman told the Times.

Freeman has provided expert testimony more than 1,200 times in many civil and criminal cases, including “injury and death litigation, automotive and other product liability, toxic tort litigation, life expectancy, and medical negligence cases, as well as in homicide, assault, and other criminal matters,” his Trial Guides background states.

He has also written extensively on injury and cause of death, publishing more than 220 scientific papers, books, and book chapters including a 2020 forensic analysis of an unexpected teen suicide, according to his website.

“He has published research on the topics of traffic crash-related injury and death, injury biomechanics and injury causation, genocide, cancer epidemiology, chronic pain mechanisms, and adult autologous stem cell therapy, among others,” Freeman’s website says. (RELATED: Here’s What Republicans’ Long-Awaited Epstein Report Shows)

Now, Freeman is trying to publish his complete findings on his analysis of Epstein’s death but in a peer-reviewed journal, but has been rejected so far, the Times reported.

The scientist found that the noose did not leave a smooth, consistent line on Epstein’s neck that slanted to a peak, as in a textbook hanging — but that the mark was deep, ragged and branched into a Y-shape on one side, per the outlet.

Freeman presented his findings at the Middle Temple, a London legal society, on Monday where he argued that Mr. Epstein’s injuries are most plausibly explained by homicidal strangulation as injuries on the body suggest there was a struggle, the outlet said.

The New York City medical examiner’s office, which performed the autopsy, told the Times that it “stands by its determination” of suicide.

Much information that medical examiners would normally use to determine a cause of death was unavailable as the examiner was not permitted to inspect the cell after Epstein’s death, the Times said. This means the autopsy photographs were some of the only concrete evidence presented in the case.

Epstein’s brother Mark published the autopsy photos of the notorious financier online after he gave them to Freeman last November.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by AMY OSBORNE/AFP via Getty Images)

New York City’s Democratic Socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, announced the disbanding of the city’s anti-riot task force — a move reminiscent of policies in other blue cities that experienced takeovers, injuries, and property damage during Antifa and Black Lives Matter riots.

Mamdani fulfilled his campaign promise Monday, announcing plans to move the Strategic Response Group (SRG) away from handling protests. Instead, the city will establish a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD) within the mayor’s office and a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) within the Police Department. (RELATED: Blue State Utility Wants To Raise Power Rates By More Than Half, Blames Wildfire Costs)

New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé, who led the bill calling for these changes, said long guns, tear gas, kettling, and pepper spray will not be used as “crowd control tactics during First Amendment activities.”

“We are building a new approach to public safety—one where all communities can trust that their safety and fundamental freedoms will be protected,” Mamdani said.

We are disbanding the SRG. https://t.co/VRMUiSQlxY

While Mamdani’s plan to create a civilian-led protest response and impose a blanket ban on anti-riot tools may be unprecedented, other cities have implemented similar policies only to reverse them after struggling to control protests that overwhelmed their resources.

“The rioters in NYC are leftists—from his political side. They’re henchmen for his political cause,” Andy Ngo, a leading journalist and New York Times best-selling author on American Antifa, said in response to the announcement. “It’s not surprising the mayor is pulling back a law enforcement response for when they turn violent.”

“Democrats made similar leadership decisions during the deadly 2020 BLM-Antifa riots. And then lectured us about the rule of law,” Ngo added.

Ngo has experienced similar failures firsthand, having been beaten by Antifa on the streets of Portland, Oregon, in 2019.

The rioters in NYC are leftists—from his political side. They’re henchmen for his political cause. It’s not surprising the mayor is pulling back a law enforcement response for when they turn violent. Democrats made similar leadership decisions during the deadly 2020 BLM-Antifa riots. And then lectured us about the rule of law.

In 2021, approximately 50 members of the Portland Police Bureau’s Rapid Response Team (RRT) resigned following a grand jury indictment of an RRT officer for assault during a 2020 protest and new state restrictions on tear gas and impact munitions, OPB reported.

Portland tried to fill the gap by using regular patrol officers and state police to cover major demonstrations over the next few years, but ultimately failed as resources were strained.

By March 2024, amid concerns about renewed civil unrest as the election approached, the Portland City Council relented. It voted to reinstate a 50-member specialized public order unit and approved a 6 percent pay increase for its officers, according to OPB.

The protests and riots had already resulted in millions of dollars in damage. That included $1.6 million in damage to the federal courthouse in 2021 and another $4.8 million in costs from looting, fires, and graffiti following a monthlong demonstration in 2020.

Between May and July 2020, 62.5 percent of Portland’s demonstrations resulted in some form of violence, according to the Major Cities Chiefs Association. Ngo also said he fled Portland following death threats in 2021.

Portland: Antifa & BLM smash buildings, they go in to loot, then they set it on fire. #antifa #BlackLivesMatter https://t.co/nj0ah9VO1z

Seattle experienced similar consequences following the 2020 establishment of the “Capitol Hill Occupied Protest” (CHOP), an autonomous zone maintained by protesters after police vacated the East Precinct.

Rather than broadly dispersing demonstrators, authorities prioritized dialogue and targeted arrests. The approach backfired as emergency response broke down, leading to shootings and several deaths at or near CHOP during the 23-day occupation.

Seattle also agreed to pay $3.65 million to settle a class-action lawsuit brought by business owners, landlords, and residents in 2023. The city additionally faced separate multimillion-dollar wrongful death claims brought by the families of teenagers killed inside CHOP.

Minneapolis also considered dismantling its police force following the 2020 death of George Floyd. A veto-proof majority of the City Council pledged to replace the Minneapolis Police Department with a public-health-oriented Department of Community Safety. However, voters rejected the charter amendment in November 2021.

Wearing heavy protective gear, cops formed a barricade as other workers cleared out the Capitol Hill Occupied Protest area in Seattle, which had recently seen a flurry of gun violence that left two Black teenagers dead https://t.co/OHZ14NqoNh https://t.co/5olIJE7Ymi

New York City has relied on the SRG during its own periods of unrest. During the city’s 2020 riots, the unit served as the NYPD’s primary rapid-response force, helping halt commercial looting in Manhattan and the Bronx by enforcing citywide curfews and clearing demonstrators during street takeovers.

University administrators also called on the SRG to clear unauthorized encampments at several colleges during the 2024-2025 campus occupations accompanying the “Free Palestine” protests.

URGENT: COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY JUST CALLED THE NYPD SRG TO MASS ARREST DOZENS OF STUDENTS teenagers, muslim, Jewish, black & brown students all arrested by @Columbia https://t.co/Sb2XM8DBYz

Beyond demonstrations, the SRG was routinely deployed to precincts experiencing spikes in shootings and violent crime. It also responded to active shootings, bank robberies in progress, and urgent searches for missing persons across the city.

While the SRG will fulfill its counterterrorism role on paper, the city will instead rely on the civilian-led CDDD to negotiate with protesters and de-escalate riots, with the Police Department’s FAST serving as a liaison to the mayor’s office. (RELATED: Mamdani’s Housing Plan Could Create Army Of Left-Wing Real Estate Barons)

Combined with the removal of tools used to control riots, the changes could leave New York City with fewer resources to respond to the consequences of policies that other Democratic-led cities have already reversed.

DEAR ABBY: I was in a relationship with a married man for more than 20 years. A year ago, I found out he was cheating on me, so I ended the relationship. We have four children under the age of 18, and our relationship has caused them nothing but heartache because he chose his wife over them.

I was so blinded by having the family I yearned for that I didn’t see how toxic the relationship was to everyone. I’m working toward building a better relationship with my children, but I think it’s hard for them to trust me because of my previous refusal to end my involvement with him. Do you have any suggestions besides time to bring us closer? — BLINDED BY HIM IN THE NORTH

DEAR BLINDED: Did you really tell your children that your lover had chosen his wife over them? If you did, it was heartless. They had nothing to do with his unwillingness to commit to you, and for the sake of their self-esteem you should make that clear.

Family counseling might help bring you closer to your children. It may also help you come to terms with the fact that you wasted so many years on this man — and understand why you did it — so you can move on. If you can manage that, there’s hope that they can, too.

DEAR ABBY: We recently did a favor for a young couple who work for us. We were happy to do it and did not expect or want any type of repayment. They decided to thank us with a nice gift of tickets to an event that takes place on a day when we are unavailable. In addition, it is three hours away from us, and, due to my mobility issues, we cannot take a long trip in the car. It’s also not something we would normally be interested in.

It seems strange and random that someone would give us such a gift, not knowing if we’re available, interested or able. I graciously thanked them for the gift and told them that we’re not going to be able to use it and why. I suggested that they try to give it to somebody else who can use the tickets. They were not cheap! I’m feeling bad now for rejecting the gift. But if we had accepted it and pretended we were going to like and use it, it would have been a lie. Did I do the right thing? — RETHINKING REJECTION

DEAR RETHINKING: When you receive a material gift in a reasonable price range, it’s usually best to accept it politely and not explain why you can’t or won’t use it. However, because these were pricey tickets to an event, and accepting would have deprived someone else of the ability to attend, you did exactly the right thing. The key is to be prompt and polite in your refusal, which you were. Imagine the awkwardness if you had lied and they later asked whether you had enjoyed yourselves at the event!

news.originalTitle: How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria
news.title: How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria
news.originalSummary:
How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria

Dozens of women sift through the waste left behind by lithium miners in Nigeria, digging for traces of ore to resell. Nigeria’s lithium industry is estimated to be worth over $34bn, but these workers only take home about $15 a week. In collaboration with Light Oriye Tamunotonye.

news.originalContent:
The IRGC says the attack is part of efforts to counter ‘hostile activities of US forces in the region’.

A drone attack has been thwarted in Bahrain, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched the barrage.

The IRGC said on Tuesday that it carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain.

The reported attacks in Bahrain – which is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has spread across the region.

It is the latest of several Iran-claimed attacks on US radar systems in the Gulf country in recent days.

The IRGC said the attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, according to a statement carried by Iran’s IRIB broadcaster.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital Manama after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Interior Ministry’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”.

On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions.

On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or injuries.

Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

news.originalContent:
Ronaldo’s mother Dolores Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat after her son had been ‘deceived’ by him.

Portugal coach Jorge Jesus believes he will still be responding to questions about Cristiano Ronaldo next year, after he was asked for his thoughts on scathing comments by the football great’s mother.

“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus asked on Tuesday, addressing the media before Portugal’s final Nations League group fixture away to Wales.

“I don’t know when it is going to stop. If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”

Jesus’s frustration stemmed from his lingering tensions with Ronaldo following the recent international retirement of football’s all-time greats.

The 72-year-old head coach responded to comments from Ronaldo’s mother in the wake of the team’s latest defeat – their first since the 41-year-old forward quit national duties.

Jesus wondered when he would stop being peppered about Ronaldo after a 4-1 Nations League defeat to Denmark prompted criticism from the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s mother, Dolores Aveiro.

Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat since taking charge after the World Cup as Ronaldo had been “deceived” by the former Benfica boss.

Ronaldo’s decision to hang up his boots for country followed a falling out with Jesus, who was previously the superstar’s coach at Saudi club Al-Nassr.

The ex-Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus star accused Jesus of broken promises after he was asked to warm up during a match against Norway in September without being introduced as a substitute.

Ronaldo left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and a token fine.

He apologised and was expected to return to the Portugal squad, but instead brought down the curtain on a 23-year international career.

His 234 appearances and 146 goals are both world records in the men’s game.

Ronaldo’s lack of mobility was often pinpointed as a factor in a richly talented Portugal squad falling short in recent major tournaments.

Jesus’s side had made a perfect start with four consecutive wins prior to Saturday’s shock defeat to the Danes.

“After the game against Denmark, everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here,” added Jesus.

“We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.”

Portugal only need a point in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League group A4 against a Wales side that will finish bottom of the section.

“You were all having a go at him for playing, and then as soon as he retires, suddenly it’s all hell breaking loose!” Wales boss Craig Bellamy told the Portuguese media.

“He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We’re all going to miss him.”

Portugal coach Jorge Jesus believes he will still be responding to questions about Cristiano Ronaldo next year, after he was asked for his thoughts on scathing comments by the football great’s mother.

“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus asked on Tuesday, addressing the media before Portugal’s final Nations League group fixture away to Wales.

“I don’t know when it is going to stop. If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”

Jesus’s frustration stemmed from his lingering tensions with Ronaldo following the recent international retirement of football’s all-time greats.

The 72-year-old head coach responded to comments from Ronaldo’s mother in the wake of the team’s latest defeat – their first since the 41-year-old forward quit national duties.

Jesus wondered when he would stop being peppered about Ronaldo after a 4-1 Nations League defeat to Denmark prompted criticism from the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s mother, Dolores Aveiro.

Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat since taking charge after the World Cup as Ronaldo had been “deceived” by the former Benfica boss.

Ronaldo left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and a token fine.

His 234 appearances and 146 goals are both world records in the men’s game.

Ronaldo’s lack of mobility was often pinpointed as a factor in a richly talented Portugal squad falling short in recent major tournaments.

news.originalContent:

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani drew widespread criticism on Monday after he announced that he would dissolve the specialized New York City Police Department counterterror unit, which also manages crowds during protests, and replace it with a civilian-led “community dialogue and de-escalation division” and a “First Amendment support team.”

City Hall called the de-escalation division a “first-of-its-kind” and said that it “will not have weapons or arrest powers.”

“During our campaign, I promised New Yorkers that we would disband the Strategic Response Group and separate counterterrorism from protest response, and today we are delivering on that promise,” Mamdani said.

“New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat,” he said. “We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation.”

The NYPD Strategic Response Group was formed in 2015.

Police officers can still be “called upon to come make arrests, including for those engaging in civil disobedience,” Mamdani said.

The new civilian-led unit will “not have weapons or arrest powers,” and the NYPD support team “will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation,” according to City Hall.

It added that police won’t be allowed to use tear gas or pepper spray during “First Amendment activities,” and that “kettling,” a crowd-control tactic in which officers confine protesters to a restricted space, will end.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said that she “would never support changes that diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat.”

“These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department,” she said.

Inna Vernikov, a member of the New York City Council and co-chair of its bipartisan task force on Jew-hatred, told JNS that “by disbanding the SRG, Mamdani is also unleashing a monster on Jewish New Yorkers.”

“Our community has already endured violent protesters attacking Jewish-owned businesses, intimidating congregants at synagogues and threatening Jewish students on university campuses,” she said. “Apparently, that’s not enough.”

“What’s another target painted on the backs of New York’s Jews for this mayor?” Vernikov told JNS.

Evan R. Bernstein, CEO of B’nai B’rith International, told JNS that the mayor’s decision is “a dangerous and ideological betrayal of public safety, especially for New York’s Jewish community.”

“At a moment when Jews remain the city’s most targeted group for hate crimes, the SRG has been one of the few specialized units capable of rapidly containing violent, antisemitic protests that have repeatedly targeted synagogues, Jewish institutions and ordinary New Yorkers,” he said.

“Replacing trained officers with an unarmed, civilian ‘dialogue’ division that has no arrest powers is not reform. It is willful blindness,” Bernstein said. “Dialogue does not stop mobs chanting for intifada or blocking streets outside of Jewish neighborhoods.”

Mamdani’s decision follows calls from anti-Israel groups, which have staged protests outside synagogues and Jewish institutions across the Big Apple, to nix the NYPD unit.

In May, an anti-Israel protest outside a Brooklyn synagogue led to multiple arrests, and an NYPD officer was hospitalized after anti-Israel protesters tried to remove barriers outside Park East Synagogue in Manhattan.

The city recorded an 182% increase in anti-Jewish hate crimes in January, in Mamdani’s first month as mayor, and since then, more than half of the city’s hate crimes have targeted Jews, who make up about 10% of New Yorkers.

Last month, 57.8% of hate crimes in New York City targeted Jews, according to city data. Jewish leaders in the city and nationwide have told JNS that the mayor’s rhetoric, including his frequent and widespread criticism of Israel, has made Jews less safe.

Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun, a Modern Orthodox synagogue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, told JNS that the mayor’s decision will have a negative impact on Jews.

“At issue is not protest as free speech. That must be sacrosanct,” the rabbi said. “What is of deep concern to the Jewish community is protest as intimidation.”

At recent demonstrations outside the UJA building and Park East Synagogue, protesters intimidated Jews, according to Steinmetz.

“Zohran Mamdani is acting like the protester-in-chief, not the mayor of New York,” he told JNS. “Because of that, there will be many more events like Park East Synagogue.”

“When there is violence,” he said, “it will be Mamdani’s fault.”

The World Jewish Congress told JNS that it has “every confidence” in the NYPD’s ability to protect Jews despite the changes.

“Politics must never get in the way of protecting Jewish lives,” it said.

Moshe Davis, former executive director of the mayor’s office to combat Jew-hatred under Mayor Eric Adams, told JNS that “we need more cops and faster responses when mobs target our community.”

“I hope this fancy video and rebrand won’t change that,” Davis, who leads the Protecting Worship coalition, told JNS. “If the mayor’s new de-escalation unit can convince his own allies to stop targeting houses of worship, we’ll all welcome it.”

Jim Geraghty, senior political correspondent at National Review, addressed the Mamdani decision on his podcast “Three Martini Lunch.”

“You’ve basically announced this is your permission slip,” he said. “This doesn’t work in other cities. Why it would work in New York is completely beyond me, but it feels very on brand for Mamdani to say, ‘I’m going to do everything I can to make my city feel more chaotic and more like an angry mob is really in control.’”

news.originalContent:
The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society.

Fifty years ago, Alain Peyrefitte, who served as a spokesperson for French President Charles de Gaulle, published a book entitled Le Mal français (The French Malaise). In the book, Peyrefitte wrote that the progress of the French nation was impeded by the lack of trust – within society and between society and state institutions. In reaction, the state exercised excessive control through rules, bureaucracy and centralisation, which resulted in stagnation.

Today, the French malaise persists, but its symptoms are quite different from the ones observed by Peyrefitte. We now have the dramatic protests by French students as well as workers and other disaffected groups, which at times have turned violent.

But these demonstrations are only the tip of the iceberg. The malaise runs much deeper.

Following the events of October 17, in which symbols of state authority were attacked – including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille and an official building in Lyon – and businesses were looted, French President Emmanuel Macron stated that these acts sought “to tear down our institutions”.

The use of such strong words reminds one of the rhetoric employed by the French government during the protests of May 1968, when students challenged the established order, and their actions were portrayed as an “attack on the Republic”.

There is, in fact, a tendency to compare the current wave of demonstrations with the events of May 1968. Yet the two movements differ. The protesters of 1968 were calling for more freedom, while today’s protesters are demanding equality and dignity. The former demonstrations were led by privileged youth; the latter are driven by those who have been left behind.

Perhaps a more relevant episode to examine is the upheaval of 2005 in the suburbs of Paris and other major cities following the deaths of two teenagers, Bouna and Zyed, who were pursued by the police.

For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation.

Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts.

The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality.

In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens.

It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour.

It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right.

In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another.

This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left).

It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around.

The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled.

In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise.

Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty.

The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”.

And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality. While those in power demand that people of immigrant background “integrate”, very little is done by the state to actually drive this process.

As a result, some French citizens feel they are French only on paper. They understand that citizenship cannot be reduced to a political discourse. Without genuine access to rights, which necessarily entails social justice and human dignity, there can be no meaningful citizenship.

In 2005, a group of activists went as far as declaring themselves the “Natives of the Republic” and calling for its decolonisation. Indeed, anyone familiar with French society can recognise that France has reproduced a colonial order within.

The country that gave birth to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has failed to treat some of its own people as full citizens. And that stands at the core of the new French malaise.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Teresa Giudice is spilling the tea on a “rude” interaction she once had with “a well-known actress.”

In her new memoir, “The Queen of New Jersey,” out now, the Bravo star recalls a time when her PR team allegedly had her pose with the celebrity while in Los Angeles for an appearance with Mario Lopez.

After they took a photo together, Giudice claims the female actress — whose name she did not reveal — asked her reps, “Why are you making me take a picture with that woman?”

Giudice, 54, went on to recall the actress having a “surprising” tone when she made the alleged comment.

“Look, I get if she didn’t know who I was, but to me, that’s just so rude,” the “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star writes.

Giudice adds that a few years later, she and her husband, Louie “Luis” Ruelas, were having dinner in LA when a girl walked in and asked the reality star for a picture.

Ten minutes later, the actress walked into the same restaurant.

“We made brief eye contact — there was definitely no need to say hi — as she was shown to her table,” Giudice writes.

Ironically, the actress was meeting the girl who had just fangirled over Giudice.

“I hope she enjoyed feigning interest as her friend showed her the pictures we’d taken just moments before,” Giudice says.

The mom of four notes that as someone in the public eye, she can’t stand stars who are publicly rude to fans.

“There are a lot of people in this business who can’t stand to stop and pose for a photo or sign something for a fan. Like, really?” she writes. “You think you’re such a big deal that you can’t spare a moment for the very audience whose attention made you who you are?”

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Want more celebrity and pop culture news?

Later in her book, Giudice, who has been on television since 2009, says fans are her “real boss.”

“I’ll admit that sometimes people take things too far and get a little too obsessed or invasive,” she acknowledges. “Everyone has to have some sort of boundary, and there’s a level of human decency that should apply to your interactions with any person, no matter how famous.”

Giudice adds, “But for the most part, my fans really are the loveliest people. I’ve met fans all over the world, and it is always the best part of my job.”

Giudice also revisits “the biggest triumphs, heartbreaks, feuds and controversies of her life with newfound perspective” in “The Queen of New Jersey,” according to an official description for the memoir.

She writes about everything from her divorce with ex-husband Joe Giudice and his deportation to her father’s death, her love story with Ruelas and more.

“The Queen of New Jersey” is out now.

“There are a lot of people in this business who can’t stand to stop and pose for a photo or sign something for a fan. Like, really?” she writes. “You think you’re such a big deal that you can’t spare a moment for the very audience whose attention made you who you are?”

Later in her book, Giudice, who has been on television since 2009, says fans are her “real boss.”

“I’ll admit that sometimes people take things too far and get a little too obsessed or invasive,” she acknowledges. “Everyone has to have some sort of boundary, and there’s a level of human decency that should apply to your interactions with any person, no matter how famous.”

Giudice adds, “But for the most part, my fans really are the loveliest people. I’ve met fans all over the world, and it is always the best part of my job.”

She writes about everything from her divorce with ex-husband Joe Giudice and his deportation to her father’s death, her love story with Ruelas and more.

news.originalContent:
The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations before to retain power. But he may find it hard this time.

Akiva Eldar is an Israeli author and was formerly an editorial writer and columnist for Haaretz.

I have been covering Benjamin Netanyahu for more than 30 years. I was in Washington when, as a young opposition leader, he worked hand in glove with the Republicans to embarrass Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and sabotage the Oslo Accords. I have seen him cornered before. I have never seen him cornered like this.

The numbers are merciless. His bloc won 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Sixty-seven members of the new Knesset recommended former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who now has up to 42 days to form a government. For Netanyahu, they may be the longest 42 days of his political life.

The stakes are political, but above all personal. His corruption trial continues, and he faces a possible prison sentence. His pardon request has been gathering dust on President Isaac Herzog’s desk for months. Eisenkot’s bloc has already tabled bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and for prime-ministerial term limits.

A state inquiry would strip him of the title he covets the most: “defender of Israel”. For Netanyahu, the chair is not a job. It is a lifeline. His trial, under way since May 2020, is in its final stretch. A sitting prime minister can be removed only after a final conviction.

From his office, he can stall hearings and lean on the justice system. Out of office, he is just another defendant.

To survive, Netanyahu does not need to build a government. He needs time to keep his rivals from building one. To buy it, he is pulling three levers.

The first is his proposal for a “national unity government” of all the parties that support Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Translation: the Arab parties, representing 21 percent of the population, are out. The Jewish supremacists, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are in. So are the anti-Zionist Haredi parties. This is unity, Netanyahu-style.

He has gift-wrapped the offer in the old rhetoric of the Iranian nuclear threat, with one catch: He would not give up the premiership or agree to a rotation.

Eisenkot has called the offer “another spin”, yet he has agreed to negotiate with Likud. He knows a refusal would only feed the spin machine: They will talk to Arab supporters of Hamas, but not to Jewish patriots, the Netanyahu camp would claim.

He also knows to beware of a diversion designed to burn through the days the president has allotted him.

The second lever is incitement. At the Knesset’s opening session, Netanyahu branded Ra’am and the Joint List “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel”. A government depending on them, he declared, “must not be formed”. The goal is to strangle an Arab-backed government in its cradle, and to scare the Haredi parties, which are currently part of his bloc, away from joining the “enemy”.

But this time the incitement has a hole in it. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas says Netanyahu’s confidant Natan Eshel sounded him out on the bill to bar an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi went on live television with WhatsApp messages he said came from Eshel. “Terror supporters”, it seems, are good enough for a quiet chat.

The third lever is escalation. According to media reports, Netanyahu has been pressing US President Donald Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran. A return to full-scale war could help him form an emergency government.

In a media interview, former Prime Minister Ehud Barak laid out the scenario: a blatant provocation that forces Iran to respond, and a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government. Lebanon, Gaza or the West Bank could serve just as well. The mantra is well-known: The enemy must see that we are united.

Here, too, there are limits. A former chief of staff of the army, Eisenkot spent many years in uniform and has no shortage of sources in the army. They are likely telling him there is no urgent need for another round of war with Iran. And Trump has hinted that he wants that war over.

If all three levers fail, Netanyahu has a familiar fallback: another election, next spring. Between 2019 and 2022, he dragged Israelis to the polls five times rather than give up the chair. Tibi has revealed that one of Netanyahu’s ministers tried to convince him his party would be better off “going to elections” than joining Eisenkot’s bloc.

Eisenkot has a problem of his own. He campaigned on three pledges: no Netanyahu, no Haredi parties, no Arab parties. He cannot keep all three. Politics is the art of choosing which promise to break.

The first path available to Eisenkot runs through the Haredim. His bloc has 48 seats; Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) would add 13, for exactly 61, the number he needs to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. A softened draft law is reportedly on the table. But UTJ’s rabbis want all 48 members of the bloc to sign a pledge exempting Haredim from military service, with an override clause to shield the law from the Supreme Court. Eisenkot has pledged not to back down on military service for all.

The second path is a minority government, backed by the Arab parties from outside the coalition. Eisenkot is reportedly willing to do it, and so is one of his allies, Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats. Another ally, Naftali Bennett, is believed to oppose it. The big obstacle is Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, who rules out the Arab parties, a minority government and new elections. Three noes in a single breath.

The third path is Likud without Netanyahu, or with him in a diplomatic role. No Likud lawmaker has broken ranks so far. And for Netanyahu, a junior partnership would be not a retirement plan but a launching pad: From inside the cabinet, he could stall the bills on a state inquiry and term limits, undermine the government and bring it down at a moment of his choosing. Just ask Benny Gantz, whose 2020 rotation deal with Netanyahu never brought him to the prime minister’s chair.

This is a game of chicken. Netanyahu is betting that Eisenkot’s partners will squabble over the draft, the Arab parties and the portfolios until the clock runs out, forcing a seventh election since 2019 — one he would fight from the Prime Minister’s Office, his finger on the trigger. Eisenkot’s best weapon is the one Netanyahu fears the most: a government, any government, sworn in before the 42 days are up.

Eisenkot’s camp has already taken over the Knesset building. Netanyahu’s camp will do everything it can to keep it from taking over the government buildings. They will not give up without street battles.

The last time incitement spilled into the streets, in November 1995, it ended with the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. It paved the way for the comeback of the Israeli right, led by a young, charming Revisionist.

Will November 2026 mark the end of the Netanyahu era and a return to Rabin’s path of peace?

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The dollar on Tuesday ​scaled a fresh 19-month peak against a basket of peers amid bets for more ‌aggressive policy tightening by the US Federal Reserve following hot inflation data and hawkish central bank rhetoric.

The US currency extended a 10-month high versus its Australian counterpart as a global selloff in AI stocks weighed on market sentiment, hurting ​the risk-sensitive Aussie.

A sharper-than-expected acceleration in US consumer inflation last week triggered a run of ​five straight days of gains for the US dollar index , which carried into a ⁠sixth day on Tuesday with it rising to 103.66, the highest since April 2, 2025, when ​President Trump rolled out his tariffs.

The index measures the dollar against six rivals, including the ​euro, sterling and the Japanese yen.

Traders now view a Fed interest-rate hike at the next meeting in December as a certainty, and they also lay around 4% odds on a supersized half-point increase, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. ​

A day earlier, those bets on an oversized hike were at nearly 12%. A week earlier, ​there were 16% odds for no change to policy.

Meanwhile, the tech selloff continued in Asia on Tuesday, with Japan’s Nikkei and ⁠South Korea’s KOSPI both firmly lower.

A key test for AI sentiment — which has been rocked by the sudden departure of Nvidia’s CEO, a Democratic sweep in US midterm elections and worries about a debt-fueled AI infrastructure expansion — comes with the release of Nvidia earnings later in the day.

The dollar has been ​supported by the AI ​boom as capital flowed ⁠into US markets.

“Continued AI-related capital inflows and expectations of faster Fed tightening should support the USD,” said CBA economist and currency strategist Carol Kong.

“However, erratic ​US policymaking and a sharp correction in AI-related equities pose key downside risks ​to our ⁠bullish USD outlook.”

In terms of the Fed outlook, US retail sales data later in the day could offer further clues.

The dollar edged to a fresh 18-month high of 0.84075 Swiss franc and rose slightly to 159.49 ⁠yen .

Japan’s currency ​has been hemmed in around 160 per dollar, which traders ​view as a potential trigger level for another round of intervention to support it.

The euro slipped to a new 19-month low ​of $1.0985. Sterling fell to $1.3172.

The Aussie dipped to $0.6725, the lowest since January.
